title: Pieces of Halley's comet will streak across the sky this week in a spectacular celestial display
excerpt: The Orionid meteor shower peaks October 21-22, bringing fast meteors from Halley's comet. Discover when and where to watch despite moonlight.
content:
The Orionid meteor shower peaks October 21-22, bringing fast meteors from Halley's comet. Discover when and where to watch despite moonlight.

This week, tiny pieces of Halley’s comet will burn up in Earth’s atmosphere and streak across the night sky. The Orionid meteor shower is expected to peak around October 21-22.

A bright Moon will get in the way for part of the night, so timing matters. The best views should come in the dark hours just before dawn, after the Moon has set.

Dust from a famous comet

Every October, Earth passes through a stream of dust and rock left behind by Halley’s comet. When those particles hit the atmosphere at high speed, they burn up and create the bright streaks we call meteors.

Halley’s comet orbits the Sun about once every 76 years, according to NASA. Casual observers last saw it in 1986, and it will not return to the inner solar system until 2061.

The comet’s debris produces two meteor showers a year. The Eta Aquariids appear in May, and the Orionids arrive in October.

That means the Orionids offer a way to see material from Halley’s comet decades before the comet itself comes back.

When the shower peaks

The Orionids are active from early October to early November, according to the American Meteor Society. The peak is expected on October 21-22.

EarthSky puts the predicted maximum at 18:00 UTC on October 21, which is 2 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time. The shower has a broad peak, so several mornings around that date can be good.

That prediction comes from the Observer’s Handbook of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada, which EarthSky cites. In practice, the mornings of October 21 and 22 are the ones to target in North America.

Under dark skies with no Moon, observers can expect about 10 to 20 meteors per hour, EarthSky says. In some exceptional years, rates have reached 50 to 75 meteors per hour.

NASA gives a slightly higher figure, about 23 meteors per hour under moonless skies. Either way, patience pays off, since the shower plays out over hours rather than minutes.

Working around the Moon

This year, a bright waxing gibbous Moon will be in the sky after midnight during the peak. Its light will wash out the fainter meteors.

The Moon sets a few hours before dawn, which leaves a window of darker sky. That is when the radiant, the point the meteors seem to come from, is high in the sky.

The full Moon follows on October 26, so the skies will only get brighter after the peak. Night skies can surprise observers in other ways too, such as the red auroras seen over Japan during recent solar storms.

Where to look

The Orionids get their name from their radiant, which lies in the constellation Orion, north of the bright star Betelgeuse. It rises before midnight and is highest around 2 a.m.

You do not need to look straight at Orion. NASA suggests looking 45 to 90 degrees away from the radiant, where meteors appear longer.

In the Northern Hemisphere, NASA recommends lying on your back with your feet pointing southeast. That lets you take in as much of the sky as possible.

Observers in the Southern Hemisphere can do the same with their feet pointing northeast. EarthSky notes that the radiant sits near Orion’s raised club, not far from Betelgeuse.

No telescope or binoculars are needed. The goal is to see as much open sky as possible with the naked eye.

Why the meteors are so fast

Orionid meteors travel at about 41 miles (66 kilometers) per second, or about 148,000 miles per hour, according to NASA.

That is only about 3 miles (5 kilometers) per second slower than the Leonids, which peak in November, Space.com reports.

The comet’s official name is 1P/Halley. Each grain of its dust that enters the atmosphere at these speeds heats up and glows as it burns away.

Tips for a better view

Find a spot well away from city and street lights. NASA advises bringing a blanket, sleeping bag or lawn chair so you can stay comfortable while you watch.

Give your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the dark, NASA says. After that, more of the fainter meteors become visible.

NASA’s general advice for this shower is to start watching after midnight and keep looking until dawn. This year, the darkest part of that window will come after the Moon goes down.

Check the weather, since clouds can hide the whole show. If the peak morning is cloudy, the following mornings can still produce meteors.

Earth.com has followed past October skies, including a year when the Orionids shared the sky with a supermoon and a bright comet. Scientists are also still learning how our own Moon formed.

The information was obtained from NASA and EarthSky.
